Alms means money, food, clothing, or any other goods given freely to poor or needy people out of charity or compassion. If you hand a coin to a beggar on the street, or give food to a homeless person, what you are giving is alms.

The single most important idea in this word is voluntary generosity toward those in need. Alms are never a payment, never a trade, and never given under force. They come entirely from the giver's own will — driven by kindness, sympathy, or a sense of moral or religious duty.

Alms can be:

  • Money — coins, cash, any monetary gift to the poor
  • Food — bread, a meal, groceries given to someone who is hungry
  • Clothing — garments given to someone who lacks them
  • Other necessities — medicine, shelter, firewood — essentially, any basic need met through an act of giving

The form of alms matters less than the spirit behind it: relief for someone who is suffering or deprived.

• The giver is typically someone with more resources — a wealthy person, a passerby, a community, or a religious institution.
  • The receiver is someone poor, destitute, homeless, sick, or otherwise unable to provide for themselves.

Historically, alms were given to beggars at the street, to monks and pilgrims, and to the sick in hospitals run by churches. In many societies, giving alms was considered a sacred duty — not just a nice gesture, but a moral obligation.

The word "alms" is deeply woven into religious traditions across the world.

  • In Christianity, giving alms is one of the three foundational acts of faith (along with prayer and fasting). It is seen as an act of love for one's neighbor.
  • In Islam, zakat (obligatory charity) and sadaqah (voluntary charity) are forms of alms. Giving to the poor is one of the Five Pillars of Islam.
  • In Hinduism and Buddhism, giving alms — especially food to monks or the needy — is considered a virtuous act that accumulates spiritual merit.

So when you encounter this word in religious texts or traditional literature, it almost always carries this moral and spiritual weight.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

A few natural examples:

  • "The old monk walked through the village, asking for alms from the households."
  • "She gave alms to the beggar who sat outside the temple every morning."
  • "In medieval times, the church was responsible for distributing alms to the poor."
  • "He lived entirely on alms, with no income of his own."

Notice the phrase "give alms" or "ask for alms" — these are the two most common verb combinations.

Alms is always written with an "s" — there is no singular form "alm." You cannot say "I gave him an alm." You say "I gave him alms" or "I gave him some alms." Even when referring to a single coin or piece of bread given in charity, you still say "alms." Think of it like the word "news" — it looks plural but functions as a single concept.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Alms" is a somewhat formal and old-fashioned word in everyday modern English. In casual conversation today, people are more likely to say "donation," "charity," or simply "gave money to a beggar." However, alms remains very much alive in:

  • Religious literature and sermons
  • Historical writing and classical novels
  • Formal discussions of charity and poverty
  • Phrases like "almsgiving" and "almshouse"

Almsgiving simply means the act of giving alms — the practice itself. An almshouse (or poorhouse) was a building, historically funded by charity, where the poor and elderly could live rent-free.
How Alms Differs from Similar Words

ConceptKey Difference
AlmsGiven specifically to the poor/needy; often has a moral or religious character
GiftGiven to anyone for any reason — a birthday present is a gift, not alms
DonationA broader, more modern word; can be given to causes, organizations, or people
CharityThe broader spirit or act of giving; alms are a specific expression of charity

Alms is narrower than "donation" or "gift" — it always implies a giver with means and a receiver in need.

Alms = things (money, food, goods) freely given to the poor, out of compassion or religious duty, with no expectation of anything in return.

If you remember just one sentence: to give alms is to help someone destitute — not because you have to, but because it is the right thing to do.
